summary: Whitney Cox works in Indology and religious studies. He studied at the University of Virginia (~1994–1998) and the University of Chicago (~2000–2006) under Sheldon Pollock (~2001–2006), and held a post at the University of Chicago (attested 2003).

Wijesinghe Sugathadasa Karunaratne (1928–1986) worked in Buddhist studies and philosophy. He studied at the University of Peradeniya and SOAS University of London (PhD ~1952–1956). He taught at Peradeniya (1952–1973) and the University of Kelaniya (~1957–1986).
Wilburn Hansen works in religious studies and Japanology. He pursued a master's program at the University of Colorado and studied at Stanford University under Bernard Faure and Carl Bielefeldt.

Wilfred Cantwell Smith (1916–2000) specialized in religious studies. He studied at Toronto, Cambridge, and Princeton (PhD ~1946–1948). He held posts at Forman Christian College (1940–1946), McGill University (1948, 1951), and Harvard University (1964–1973, 1978–1985).

Wilfrid Sellars (1912–1989) was a philosopher who studied at Michigan, Buffalo, Göttingen, and Oxford. He taught at Iowa (1938–1946), Minnesota (1947–1958), and Yale (1958–1963), before serving as professor at Pittsburgh (1963–1989).

Wilhelm Deecke (1831–1897) worked in linguistics and Indology. He earned his doctorate at Leipzig (1848–1849) and studied at Berlin under Albrecht Weber and others (~1851–1854). He directed several schools, including Ernestinenschule (1855–1870) and Lycée de Mulhouse (1889).

Wilhelm Dilthey (1833–1911) was a philosopher who studied at Heidelberg (~1852–1853) and Humboldt University of Berlin (~1853–1856). He held posts at Basel (~1866–1868), Kiel (~1868–1871), Breslau (~1871–1882), and Berlin (~1882–1905).

Wilhelm Geiger (1856–1943) worked in Indology, Iranian and Central Asian studies, and linguistics. He earned his PhD at Erlangen-Nürnberg under Friedrich von Spiegel, later holding professorships at Erlangen-Nürnberg (1891) and the University of Munich (1920–1924).

Wilhelm Grube (1855–1908) specialized in Sinology, linguistics, and Tibetology. He studied at Saint Petersburg State University and Leipzig University (PhD 1878–1880), and held posts at the Ethnological Museum of Berlin and Humboldt University of Berlin (from 1884; professor 1892).
Wilhelm Gundert (1880–1971) was a scholar of Japanology and religious studies who succeeded Karl Florenz and held a post at the University of Hamburg (~1936–1945).

Wilhelm Halbfass (1940–2000) worked in Indology and philosophy. He studied at Vienna (~1958–1961) and Göttingen (doctorate ~1964–1967), and held posts at the University of Göttingen (~1968–1970) and the University of Pennsylvania (1982–2000).

Wilhelm Havers (1879–1961) worked in linguistics and Indology. He held academic posts at Leipzig (~1915–1917), Bern (~1917–1920), Würzburg (~1920–1929), Breslau (~1929–1937), and the University of Vienna (~1937–1953).

Wilhelm Max Müller (1862–1919) was a scholar in history, archaeology, and linguistics. He studied at Leipzig University (~1885–1888) and Humboldt University of Berlin, and held a post at the University of Pennsylvania (~1910–1919).

Wilhelm Pertsch (1832–1899) specialized in Indology and Iranian and Central Asian studies. He studied at Berlin and Tübingen under Albrecht Weber and Rudolf von Roth, later serving as librarian and director at Forschungsbibliothek Gotha and Schloss Friedenstein.
Wilhelm Printz (1887–1941) was an Indology scholar who studied under Wilhelm Schulze (~1906–1910) and Heinrich Lüders (~1909–1911).

Wilhelm Radloff (1837–1918) worked in Iranian and Central Asian studies, linguistics, and archaeology. Educated at Berlin and Jena (doctorate ~1858), he directed the Asiatic Museum (1885–1890) and the Peter the Great Museum of Anthropology and Ethnography (1894–1918).

Wilhelm Rau (1922–1999) was an Indologist and linguist. He studied at Leipzig and Marburg (doctorate 1946–1949 under Johannes Nobel), and served as professor at Goethe University Frankfurt (1955) and the University of Marburg (1958–1987).

Wilhelm Scherer (1841–1886) worked in linguistics and German studies. He studied at Vienna and Berlin, and held professorships at the University of Vienna (1868–1872), University of Strasbourg (1872), and Humboldt University of Berlin (1877).

Wilhelm Schmidt (1868–1954) was a scholar in linguistics and religious studies. He studied at Humboldt University of Berlin (~1893–1895) and held academic posts at the University of Vienna (~1921–1938) and the University of Fribourg (~1939–1951).

Wilhelm Schott (1802–1889) specialized in Sinology, Iranian and Central Asian studies, and linguistics. He studied at Humboldt University of Berlin (~1823–1826) and later held a post there (~1838–1889).
